design_note: Makes hidden-test execution a second untrusted execution surface. The same patch crosses into another sandbox, while credentials stay outside both; a trusted test definition does not sanitize candidate code.

source.title: Security Model
source.concept: Sandboxing limits exposure to untrusted code but does not replace secure architecture. Mapped files, network paths and resource controls still require deliberate policy.
source.scope: Original maintenance-agent boundaries; no sandbox product or diagram alone is claimed to enforce the shown credential and publication rules.

lesson.anchor: What changes and what stays universal
lesson.title: Hidden tests still execute untrusted code
lesson.intro: A maintenance agent submits patch P-18. A harness checks permitted paths, then evaluates that same candidate in a separate test sandbox. Hidden test definitions do not make the patched application trusted.

edges.label: Patch artifact; check paths and links
Run tests against candidate in sandbox
No credential mount or secret access

read: The path guard inspects the artifact; it does not prove the code is harmless.
The hidden runner executes the candidate inside the judge boundary.
Publication credentials remain outside candidate execution in both sandboxes.
lesson.question: Would hiding the test files justify running P-18 on the host with publication credentials?
lesson.answer: No. Candidate code can execute during testing even when test definitions are secret. Keep both ordinary and hidden checks isolated without host or publication authority, and enforce mounts, egress and resources. A permitted diff and passing tests remain review evidence, not permission to merge or publish unrelated changes.
lesson.takeaway: Keep candidate code isolated everywhere it executes, including independent evaluation.
lesson.assumption: Fictional enforced boundaries; both sandboxes exclude credentials. Network, mounts and resource controls need actual configuration and tests beyond this drawing.
